content: Erysipelas and cellulitis, collectively referred to as cellulitis, are common bacterial skin infections that predominantly affect the lower extremities. Despite the significant morbidity associated with these conditions, the evidence supporting various prevention strategies remains unclear. The objective of this review was to evaluate the benefits and potential adverse effects of antibiotic prophylaxis or other preventive interventions in reducing recurrent episodes of cellulitis in adults aged 16 years and older. To gather relevant data, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Skin Group Specialised Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, and LILACS, up to June 2016. Additional searches were performed in five trial registries, dermatology conference proceedings, and BIOSIS Previews. Reference lists of included studies and reviews were also examined for randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that evaluated therapies aimed at preventing recurrent cellulitis. The review included six RCTs with a total of 573 participants, whose average age ranged from 50 to 70 years. Participants had experienced between one and four prior episodes of cellulitis. Five of the six trials focused on antibiotic prophylaxis for cellulitis of the legs, while one trial investigated selenium for cellulitis of the arms. Among the antibiotic studies, one trial assessed oral erythromycin (32 participants), and four trials evaluated penicillin (481 participants). The duration of treatment ranged from six to 18 months, with two studies continuing follow-up for up to two years after discontinuation of prophylaxis. Four studies were conducted at single centers, while two were multicenter trials, spanning five countries: the UK, Sweden, Tunisia, Israel, and Austria. The findings indicated that antibiotic prophylaxis significantly reduced the risk of cellulitis recurrence during the treatment phase. Specifically, the risk of recurrence decreased by 69% compared to no treatment or placebo (risk ratio [RR] 0.31, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.13 to 0.72; 513 participants; P = 0.007). The number needed to treat (NNT) to prevent one additional recurrence was six (95% CI 5 to 15). The certainty of evidence for this outcome was rated as moderate. Antibiotic prophylaxis also reduced the incidence rate of cellulitis by 56% (RR 0.44, 95% CI 0.22 to 0.89; 473 participants; P = 0.02) and significantly delayed the time to the next episode of cellulitis (hazard ratio [HR] 0.51, 95% CI 0.34 to 0.78; 437 participants; P = 0.002). Both outcomes were supported by moderate-certainty evidence. However, the protective effects of antibiotics did not persist after prophylaxis was discontinued. Post-prophylaxis, there was no significant reduction in the risk of recurrence (RR 0.88, 95% CI 0.59 to 1.31; 287 participants; P = 0.52), incidence rate (RR 0.94, 95% CI 0.65 to 1.36; 287 participants; P = 0.74), or time to the next episode (HR 0.78, 95% CI 0.39 to 1.56; 287 participants). The certainty of evidence for these post-prophylaxis outcomes was low. The effects of antibiotic prophylaxis were most relevant for individuals who had experienced at least two episodes of leg cellulitis within a three-year period. No significant differences were observed between antibiotic prophylaxis and no treatment or placebo in terms of adverse effects (RR 0.87, 95% CI 0.58 to 1.30; 469 participants; P = 0.48) or hospitalizations (RR 0.77, 95% CI 0.37 to 1.57; 429 participants; P = 0.47). The certainty of evidence for these outcomes was low. Common adverse effects included gastrointestinal symptoms such as nausea and diarrhea, rash, and thrush. Severe cutaneous adverse reactions were not reported. Three studies documented adverse effects that led to treatment discontinuation. For example, in one study involving erythromycin, three participants experienced abdominal pain and nausea, prompting a switch to penicillin. In another study, two participants receiving penicillin withdrew due to diarrhea or nausea. In a third study, approximately 10% of participants discontinued treatment due to pain at the injection site associated with intramuscular benzathine penicillin. None of the included studies assessed the development of antimicrobial resistance or quality-of-life outcomes. Additionally, the available data did not allow for a thorough evaluation of the impact on hospital length of stay. Regarding the risk of bias, two studies were judged to have a low risk of bias, while three were considered to have a high risk of bias, primarily due to a lack of blinding. In conclusion, antibiotic prophylaxis appears to be an effective preventive measure for reducing the recurrence, incidence, and time to the next episode of cellulitis in individuals undergoing treatment, compared to placebo or no treatment. However, the protective effects diminish after discontinuation of antibiotics. The treatment is associated with minor adverse effects, such as nausea and rash, and does not appear to cause serious adverse events. The evidence is limited to individuals with at least two prior episodes of leg cellulitis within a three-year period. Importantly, none of the studies evaluated other common preventive measures, such as lymphoedema management or proper skin care. Larger, high-quality studies with long-term follow-up are needed to explore additional prophylactic strategies.
